newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Global debt under threat if yen turns.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Global debt under threat if yen turns.

text.p: Global bond markets are in for a blow-out if recent yen weakness is halted and the U.S. dollar is sent scuttling lower, analysts said on Tuesday.

Comments last week from an MoF minister suggested Japan has had enough of seeing the yen falter against an overpowering dollar, and raised the spectre of a reversal in this trend taking the shine off recent bond market rallies.
"It would not necessarily be fatal, but it could cause quite a decent correction in global bond markets," said Ian Amstad, senior economist at Bankers Trust in London.
Since April last year, when dollar/yen bottomed out at 79.70, the dollar has staged an impressive rally, reaching as high as 114.91 in the past few weeks.
Global bond investors have enjoyed the ride.

Borrowing in yen, where interest rates are a paltry 0.5 percent, players have plunged into higher-yielding debt markets with the currency risk limited by Japanese enthusiasm for a weak yen versus the dollar.
But the yen can no longer be treated as a one-way bet.

MoF Vice Minister Eisuke Sakakibara, known to the markets as "Mr Yen", was quoted as saying last week that the Japanese economy was stronger than market perceptions held it, and that the hour of the strong dollar was over. While analysts said a sharp reversal in the dollar's rally was unlikely in the near term, they said investors should keep watch over the next 12 months.
European high-yielders, such as Italy, Spain and Sweden would be among the main victims if the dollar were to lose its footing.
These markets traditionally gain when the dollar is strong, since the mark is left in a weaker position and units such as the lira and peseta gain ground on European crosses.

But Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase in London, and Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said Australian and New Zealand bond markets were likely to suffer the most.
"Those are the ones which are most reliant on Japanese fund flows at the moment," Schmidt said.

Baader said Japanese investors, seeing the rich rewards from the so-called "yen carry" trades beginning to be wiped out by yen appreciation, would soon revert to domestic markets, pulling large capital flows out of Treasuries, Aussie and Kiwi bonds, and European high-yielders.

"If people see their positions under threat from an appreciation in the yen, and they have suspicions that the Japanese may consider raising overnight rates, that will lead them to revserse those trades," he said.
But it is a big if -- certainly in the short term.

Amstad said dollar/yen might come under slight pressure in the near-term, saying the failure of dollar/mark to overcome resistance at 1.55 throughout 1996 may spark concerns about the sustainability of dollar strength.

The dollar recovered from two-month lows against the mark on Tuesday but was still quoted well off the 1.55 level at 1.4940/45 in European midsession business. Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp joined the currency comment party on Tuesday, saying a stronger dollar "might seem more appropriate".
Dollar/yen was quoted at 111.30/40 by 1325 GMT.

A trigger for a more substantial move -- of a potentially destructive size for global bond markets -- was unlikely to come for some time, analysts said, and could well be in the form of a monetary tightening in Japan in the first half of 1997.

"It is certainly clear that the Japanese MoF does not want the weaker yen trend to continue in the short term," said Chase's Schmidt. "But there is a long way to go from saying that to actually seeing dollar/yen move lower."
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
